Lean Foundations
What Is Lean?
Deliver what the customer values, with less waste.
Lean is a way of working that delivers what the customer values using less time, effort, space and material. It does this by removing steps that add no value and making work flow.
Observe the process. Find the gap. Improve the standard.
Lean Foundations
What Is Value?
Value is what the customer is willing to pay for.
Value is defined by the customer: the right product, at the right quality and quantity, delivered at the right time and cost. Work that moves the product toward that need adds value.
Observe the process. Find the gap. Improve the standard.
Lean Foundations
Value-Added vs Non-Value-Added
Keep the value. Reduce the necessary. Remove the waste.

Value-added (VA) work changes the product in a way the customer wants and is done right the first time. Non-value-added (NVA) work uses time or resources without adding value. Some NVA is necessary today, such as required tests and safety checks: reduce it. The rest is pure waste: eliminate it.
Observe the process. Find the gap. Improve the standard.
Lean Foundations
The 5 Lean Principles
Five steps that turn customer value into a flowing process.
The 5 Lean principles are: specify value from the customer's view, map the value stream, make the work flow, let the customer pull, and pursue perfection through continuous improvement.
Value, stream, flow, pull, perfection: in that order.
Lean Foundations
Customer Value
The customer decides what is worth paying for.

Customer value is the benefit a customer receives from a product or service compared with what they give up for it: price, waiting and effort. Improvement starts by understanding that need in the customer's own words.
Ask the customer. Do not assume what they value.
Lean Foundations
Waste in Manufacturing
Anything that uses resources but adds no customer value.

Waste (muda) is any activity that consumes time, material, space, energy or effort without adding value the customer will pay for. Removing waste lets the same team deliver more value with less effort.
If it adds no value, question why it exists.
Lean Foundations
The 8 Wastes (DOWNTIME)
Remember DOWNTIME to spot the eight wastes.
The 8 wastes are Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-utilized talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion and Extra-processing. The first letters spell DOWNTIME, an easy memory aid for waste walks.
Learn DOWNTIME, then go and find it.
Lean Foundations
Defects
Work that has to be fixed, redone or thrown away.

Defects are products or services that do not meet requirements and need rework, repair, re-inspection or scrap. Every defect consumes material, time and capacity twice and risks reaching the customer.
Prevent the defect at its source; do not just catch it.
Lean Foundations
Overproduction
Making more, or earlier, than the customer needs.

Overproduction means producing more than is needed, or before it is needed. It is often called the worst waste because it hides problems and creates other wastes: inventory, handling, space and risk of expiry.
Make what is needed, when it is needed.
Lean Foundations
Waiting
People, machines or material idle, waiting for the next step.
Waiting is any time when people, equipment or material are idle because the next step is not ready: waiting for material, approval, information, a machine or a test result.
Make waits visible, then remove their cause.
Lean Foundations
Non-Utilized Talent
Ideas, skills and experience that are never used.
Non-utilized talent is the waste of not using people's knowledge, skills and ideas. Operators often know the causes of problems best, but are not asked or not given time to improve.
The people doing the work hold the best ideas.
Lean Foundations
Transportation
Moving material more than the process needs.
Transportation waste is unnecessary movement of materials, products or information between locations. Every move adds time, cost and risk of damage without changing the product.
Shorten the route and reduce the moves.
Lean Foundations
Inventory
More material than the process needs right now.

Inventory waste is any raw material, work-in-progress or finished goods beyond what is needed for smooth flow. Excess stock ties up cash and space and hides problems such as unreliable machines or long changeovers.
Lower the water level to see the rocks.
Lean Foundations
Motion
Movement of people that adds no value.
Motion waste is unnecessary movement by people: walking, reaching, bending, searching or turning. It costs time and effort and can cause strain and injury.
Bring the work to the person, not the person to the work.
Lean Foundations
Extra-Processing
Doing more than the customer requires.
Extra-processing is any work beyond what the customer needs: extra steps, tighter-than-needed tolerances, duplicate checks or extra approvals and reports.
Match the process to the real requirement.
Lean Foundations
Waste Walk
A structured walk to see waste where work happens.
A waste walk is a planned visit to the work area to observe the process and note waste using a simple checklist such as DOWNTIME. The goal is to see and record facts, not to blame people.
Walk, observe, record, then act on the top few.
Lean Foundations
Gemba
The real place where value is created.
Gemba is a Japanese term for the actual place where work happens: the line, the warehouse, the lab. Problems are understood best where they occur, with the people who do the work.
Go to the place where the work is done.
Lean Foundations
Go and See
Go to the work. See the facts. Show respect.
Go and See (genchi genbutsu) means going to the source to confirm facts with your own eyes before deciding. It replaces assumptions and reports with direct observation.
Confirm facts at the source before deciding.
Lean Foundations
Lean Thinking
A way of thinking about value, flow and people.
Lean thinking looks at work through the customer's eyes, sees the whole process rather than single departments, and improves step by step with the people doing the work.
See the whole flow through the customer's eyes.
Lean Foundations
Lean vs Traditional Operations
Two different ways to run a factory.
Traditional operations often push large batches based on forecasts and optimize each department. Lean operations make what customers pull, keep batches small and optimize the whole flow.
Optimize the flow, not just the machine.
Lean Foundations
Flow
Work moves smoothly from step to step.
Flow means products move from one value-adding step to the next without stopping, waiting or going backwards. Good flow shortens lead time and exposes problems quickly.
Remove the stops and the work will flow.
Lean Foundations
Pull System
Produce only when the next step signals a need.
A pull system starts or replenishes work only when the downstream process or customer uses something and sends a signal, such as a kanban card or an empty bin.
Let real demand trigger the work.
Lean Foundations
Perfection Through Kaizen
Perfection is a direction, not a finish line.
Perfection, the fifth Lean principle, means continuously improving toward zero waste through many small steps (kaizen). Each improvement becomes the new standard and the next starting point.
Each standard is the base for the next improvement.
Lean Foundations
Lean Terminology
Common Lean words every team should know.

Lean uses a shared vocabulary so teams can talk about problems precisely. Key terms include gemba (the real place), muda (waste), kaizen (improvement), takt (demand pace), kanban (signal) and poka-yoke (error-proofing).
A shared language makes problems easier to discuss.
Lean Foundations
Lean Foundations Review
Value, waste, flow, pull and the people who improve them.
This month covered the core of Lean: value is defined by the customer, waste is everything else, flow and pull connect the process to demand, and kaizen at the gemba keeps improving it.
Value, waste, flow, pull, people: the Lean foundation.
Lean Foundations
Factory Waste Spotting
Train your eyes to see waste in five minutes.
Waste spotting is the practice of observing one area for a short, fixed time and listing every waste you see. Repeated often, it builds the habit of noticing what has become normal.
What looks normal is often waste.
Lean Foundations
Value Stream Basics
All the steps from order to delivery.
A value stream is the complete set of activities, value-adding and not, needed to bring a product from customer order or raw material to delivery. Seeing the whole stream shows where time is lost.
See the whole stream, not just your own step.
Lean Foundations
Lead Time vs Cycle Time
Two times that are easy to confuse.

Cycle time is the time one process step takes to complete one unit. Lead time is the total time from start (such as an order) to delivery, including all waiting. Lead time is usually much longer than the sum of cycle times.
Cut the waiting to cut the lead time.
Lean Foundations
Process vs Operation
The flow of the product versus the work of the people.
A process is the flow of material or information through steps over time. An operation is the work done by a person or machine at one point. Improving operations alone may not improve the process.
Improve the process first, then the operations.
Lean Foundations
Lean in Daily Work
Small Lean habits for every shift.
Lean in daily work means building small habits: start the shift with a short huddle, keep the workplace in order, make problems visible, follow the standard, and raise one improvement idea each week.
Small daily habits beat big occasional projects.
5S & Visual Management
What Is 5S?
Five steps to a safe, clean and organized workplace.
5S is a method for organizing the workplace: Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardize and Sustain. It removes clutter, gives everything a place, and makes abnormal conditions easy to see.
A place for everything, and everything in its place.
5S & Visual Management
Sort (Seiri)
Keep only what is needed for the work.
Sort (Seiri) means separating needed items from unneeded ones and removing what is not required for current work. It frees space and reduces searching and safety risks.
When in doubt, red-tag it.
5S & Visual Management
Set in Order (Seiton)
A clear, labelled place for every needed item.
Set in Order (Seiton) means arranging needed items so they are easy to find, use and return. Location is based on frequency of use, with labels, outlines and shadow boards.
Anyone should find any item in 30 seconds.
5S & Visual Management
Shine (Seiso)
Clean to inspect, and inspect to find problems.
Shine (Seiso) means cleaning the work area and equipment regularly, and using cleaning as inspection. Leaks, loose bolts and wear are found while cleaning.
Cleaning is inspection.
5S & Visual Management
Standardize (Seiketsu)
Make the first three S a written, visual routine.
Standardize (Seiketsu) means creating simple standards, such as checklists, photos and visual rules, so that Sort, Set in Order and Shine are done the same way by everyone, every time.
Make the right condition obvious to everyone.
5S & Visual Management
Sustain (Shitsuke)
Turn 5S into a habit that lasts.
Sustain (Shitsuke) means building the discipline to follow the 5S standards every day through audits, leader support, training and recognition.
Without Sustain, 5S slowly disappears.
5S & Visual Management
Red Tagging
A simple tag to decide what stays and what goes.
Red tagging marks items whose need is unclear during Sort. Tagged items go to a holding area for a fixed period, then are kept, relocated or disposed of by an agreed owner.
Tag it, hold it, decide it.
5S & Visual Management
5S Audit
A regular check that 5S standards are being met.
A 5S audit uses a simple scored checklist to assess each S in a zone. The score shows trends and highlights gaps; the purpose is improvement, not blame.
Audit to improve, not to blame.
5S & Visual Management
Shadow Boards
Every tool has a home you can see.
A shadow board shows the outline of each tool in its fixed place. A missing tool is visible at a glance, which saves searching and protects against loss.
An empty outline is an instant alarm.
5S & Visual Management
Visual Controls
Signals that show the normal condition at a glance.
Visual controls are signs, colours, markings and indicators that show the correct condition, so anyone can see immediately whether things are normal or not.
If it needs explaining, it is not yet visual.
5S & Visual Management
Floor Markings
Lines on the floor that organize space and flow.
Floor markings define walkways, work zones, storage locations and safety areas using agreed colours and shapes. They guide movement and make out-of-place items obvious.
Agree the colour code, then apply it everywhere.
5S & Visual Management
Labeling & Identification
Clear labels so the right item is always used.
Labeling and identification means marking materials, locations, equipment and status clearly so that people use the right item and avoid mix-ups.
Unlabelled items invite mistakes.
5S & Visual Management
Point-of-Use Storage
Store items where they are used.
Point-of-use storage keeps tools, parts and materials at the place where they are used, in the quantity needed. It reduces walking, searching and handling.
Shorten the reach, shorten the time.
5S & Visual Management
Before/After 5S
Show the change with the same view, before and after.
A before/after 5S comparison uses photos taken from the same position to show the change in an area. It makes progress visible and helps sustain the new standard.
Same angle, same place: let the photos speak.
5S & Visual Management
5S in Stores
Organized stores mean faster, error-free picking.
5S in stores organizes racks, bins and locations so materials are easy to find, count and issue in the right order, with clear labels and min/max levels.
If it cannot be found, it does not exist.
5S & Visual Management
5S in Maintenance
Find tools and parts fast when equipment stops.
5S in maintenance organizes tools, spares and workbenches so technicians can find what they need quickly during breakdowns and planned jobs.
Faster repairs start with an organized workshop.
5S & Visual Management
5S in Production
A clean line runs better and safer.
5S in production keeps lines organized, with clear material locations, clean machines and visible standards, so abnormalities are seen quickly and changeovers are faster.
Organize the line, and the line runs smoother.
5S & Visual Management
5S in Quality Lab
Order in the lab protects results.
5S in the quality lab organizes glassware, reagents, samples and instruments so tests are done correctly and on time, with clear labels and expiry control.
An organized lab gives reliable, faster results.
5S & Visual Management
Visual Management
See the status of work without asking.
Visual management makes the status of work, standards and problems visible to everyone at the place of work, so teams can see at a glance whether they are on track.
Make it visible, then make it better.
5S & Visual Management
Andon
A signal that calls for help immediately.
Andon is a visual and sometimes audible signal used to show that a process needs help, such as a light, a board or a cord. It allows problems to be raised and responded to fast.
Raise the problem fast; respond faster.
5S & Visual Management
Status Boards
Boards that show where the work stands.
Status boards display key information about work in progress, such as orders, machine status or job progress, so that the team shares one picture of the situation.
One board, one shared picture.
5S & Visual Management
Abnormality Visibility
Design the workplace so problems cannot hide.
Abnormality visibility means designing standards and visuals so that any deviation from normal stands out immediately, prompting a quick response.
Normal should look normal; abnormal should shout.
5S & Visual Management
Color Coding
One agreed colour language across the site.
Colour coding uses consistent colours to show meaning, such as status, material type or zone. It only works if the code is agreed, documented and used the same way everywhere.
Same colour, same meaning, everywhere.
5S & Visual Management
One-Point Lessons
One idea, one page, explained in minutes.
A one-point lesson (OPL) is a short visual training sheet that explains a single topic, such as a check or a method, in a few minutes at the workplace.
Teach one point at a time, at the place of work.
5S & Visual Management
5S Common Mistakes
Why many 5S programs fade after the first push.
Common 5S mistakes include treating it as a one-time clean-up, skipping Standardize and Sustain, no ownership of zones, and audits used to blame rather than improve.
5S is a habit, not an event.
5S & Visual Management
5S Sustainment
Keep 5S alive month after month.
5S sustainment relies on clear owners, short daily routines, regular audits, leaders who check and support, and recognition of teams that keep improving.
Owners, routines and leaders keep 5S alive.
5S & Visual Management
Visual Factory
A factory that tells its own status.
A visual factory uses signs, boards, markings and signals so that anyone walking through can understand what is happening, what is normal and where help is needed.
Walk through and understand without asking.
5S & Visual Management
5S Case Study
How a team brought order to a packing area.

A 5S case study follows one area through all five steps, showing the starting condition, the actions taken and how the new standard is sustained. Use measured data from your own site when you tell the story.
Tell the story with photos and your own measured results.
5S & Visual Management
5S Checklist
A quick daily check for any area.
A 5S checklist turns the standard into simple yes/no checks that any team member can complete in a few minutes, so gaps are found and fixed daily.
Five checks, five minutes, every shift.
5S & Visual Management
5S Review
Sort, Set, Shine, Standardize, Sustain, and make it visual.
This month covered 5S and visual management: organize the workplace, make the normal condition obvious, signal problems quickly, and build the habits that keep it that way.
Organize it, make it visible, keep it that way.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
What Is Kaizen?
Change for the better, a little every day.
Kaizen means continuous improvement through small, practical changes made by the people who do the work. Many small improvements, standardized and repeated, add up over time.
Small changes, made every day, by everyone.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Kaizen vs Innovation
Small steady steps versus big leaps.

Kaizen improves through many small, low-cost steps by everyone. Innovation makes larger jumps through new technology or investment. Organizations need both, and kaizen keeps gains from slipping between leaps.
Use innovation to leap; use kaizen to climb and hold.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Small Improvements
The power of many small fixes.
Small improvements are quick, low-risk changes that remove a daily irritation or waste. Because they are easy to try, more people take part and more problems get solved.
Do not wait for the big project. Fix what you can today.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
PDCA Cycle
Plan, Do, Check, Act: the learning loop.
PDCA is a four-step cycle for improvement: Plan a change based on facts, Do it on a small scale, Check the result against the plan, and Act by standardizing or adjusting. Then repeat.
Plan small, test fast, learn, standardize.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
PDSA Cycle
Same loop, with a focus on study and learning.
PDSA (Plan, Do, Study, Act) is Deming's version of the improvement cycle. 'Study' stresses comparing results with predictions and learning why, not only checking whether a target was met.
Predict, test, then study what you learned.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
A3 Problem Solving
One page that tells the whole problem story.

A3 problem solving uses a single A3-size sheet to follow a structured path: background, current condition, goal, root cause analysis, countermeasures, plan and follow-up. It keeps thinking clear and shareable.
If it does not fit on one page, the thinking is not clear yet.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Problem Statement
Describe the problem with facts, not solutions.
A problem statement describes what is wrong, where, when and how much, compared with the standard or expectation. It does not include causes or solutions.
State the gap. Leave the solution for later.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Define the Gap
Current condition versus the desired condition.
Defining the gap means measuring the current condition, stating the desired condition, and describing the difference clearly so the team knows exactly what it is trying to close.
No clear gap, no clear improvement.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Containment vs Correction
Stop the bleeding, then cure the disease.
Containment is a quick action to protect the customer from a problem, such as holding or sorting suspect stock. Correction (and corrective action) removes the cause so the problem does not return.
Contain first, but never stop at containment.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Corrective vs Preventive Action
Fix what happened, and prevent what could happen.
Corrective action removes the cause of a problem that has occurred, to prevent recurrence. Preventive action removes the cause of a potential problem before it happens.
Corrective looks back; preventive looks ahead.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Root Cause Thinking
Look past the symptom to what really caused it.
Root cause thinking means asking what condition allowed a problem to happen, and verifying it with evidence, instead of reacting only to the visible symptom.
Treat causes, not symptoms.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
5 Whys
Ask why until you reach a cause you can act on.
5 Whys is a simple method of asking 'why?' repeatedly, each answer based on facts, until a root cause is found that can be fixed. The number five is a guide, not a rule.
Each 'why' must be backed by evidence.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Fishbone Diagram
Organize possible causes before jumping to answers.

A fishbone (Ishikawa or cause-and-effect) diagram groups possible causes of a problem into categories such as Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement and Environment, so the team considers all angles.
List causes widely, then verify the few that matter.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Pareto Analysis
Find the vital few causes that matter most.

Pareto analysis ranks problems or causes by frequency or impact so the team can focus on the largest contributors first. It is based on the observation that a few causes often account for most of the effect.
Fix the biggest bars first.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Brainstorming Rules
Rules that bring out more and better ideas.
Good brainstorming sets clear rules: one topic, quantity before quality, no criticism during idea generation, build on others' ideas, and everyone gets a turn. Evaluation comes afterwards.
Generate first, judge later.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Affinity Diagram
Group many ideas into a few clear themes.
An affinity diagram organizes a large number of ideas or observations into natural groups. The team sorts notes silently, then names each group, revealing the main themes.
Sort the noise into a few themes.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Problem-Solving Team
The right people, roles and time to solve it.
A problem-solving team brings together people who know the process, the problem and the data, with a clear leader, a sponsor who removes barriers, and agreed meeting time.
Include the people closest to the problem.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Kaizen Event
A focused burst of improvement in a few days.
A kaizen event is a short, focused improvement workshop, typically lasting a few days, where a cross-functional team analyses one process, tests changes on the spot and standardizes the result.
Prepare well, act fast, follow up.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Suggestion System
A simple way for everyone to share ideas.
A suggestion system collects, reviews and implements ideas from employees. Good systems respond quickly, let people implement their own ideas where possible, and recognize contributions.
Fast responses keep ideas coming.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Standardize the Improvement
Lock in the gain so it does not slip back.
Standardizing an improvement means updating the work instruction, training everyone affected, adding visual aids and checks, so the new method becomes the normal way of working.
An improvement is not done until it is the standard.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Verify Results
Prove the improvement with before/after facts.
Verifying results means comparing measured performance before and after a change, over a long enough period, to confirm the improvement is real and the problem has not moved elsewhere.
No data, no claim.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Horizontal Deployment
Spread a good fix to every similar place.
Horizontal deployment (yokoten) shares a proven improvement with other lines, shifts or sites that have similar processes, so the same problem is prevented everywhere.
Fix it once, apply it everywhere it fits.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Kaizen Newspaper
A simple board to track improvement actions.
A kaizen newspaper is a visual list of problems and actions, showing each issue, its owner, due date and status. It keeps small improvements moving and visible.
Every action gets an owner and a date.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Kaizen Metrics
Measure the activity and the results of kaizen.
Kaizen metrics track both effort (such as ideas submitted, implemented and people involved) and outcomes (such as safety, quality, delivery and cost improvements linked to the changes).
Measure participation and results together.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Common RCA Mistakes
Traps that lead to the wrong cause.
Common root cause analysis mistakes include stopping at the first answer, blaming people, relying on opinion instead of data, and choosing a solution before the cause is verified.
'Human error' is a starting point, not a root cause.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Problem-Solving at Gemba
Solve problems where they happen.
Problem-solving at gemba means going to the actual place, observing the process and the failed part, and talking to the people involved before analyzing and deciding.
Hold the part, watch the process, ask the operator.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
A3 Example
An illustrative A3 on late batch release.
An A3 example shows how one page connects background, current condition, goal, cause analysis, countermeasures and follow-up. The facts below are an illustration; use your own data in a real A3.
Left side: understand. Right side: act and follow up.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Kaizen Case Study
An illustrative kaizen at a labelling station.
A kaizen case study shows the problem, the small changes tried and how the result was verified. This example is illustrative; replace it with measured results from your own site.
Show the before, the change and the verified after.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
PDCA in Daily Work
Use PDCA in everyday decisions, not just projects.
PDCA in daily work means treating each small change as a test: plan it, try it, check what happened at the end of the shift, and decide whether to keep, adjust or drop it.
Every day is a chance to run one small PDCA.
Kaizen & Problem Solving
Problem Solving Review
Define, analyze, fix, verify and spread.
This month covered kaizen and problem solving: state the problem with facts, contain it, find and verify the root cause, apply countermeasures with PDCA, standardize and deploy horizontally.
Facts, root cause, test, standardize, spread.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
What Is Six Sigma?
Reduce variation so every output meets the requirement.
Six Sigma is a data-driven approach to improving processes by reducing variation and defects. It uses the DMAIC method and statistical tools to find and control the causes of variation.
Less variation means fewer defects.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
What Is Lean Six Sigma?
Lean speed plus Six Sigma precision.
Lean Six Sigma combines Lean's focus on removing waste and improving flow with Six Sigma's focus on reducing variation and defects. Together they make processes faster and more reliable.
Remove waste and reduce variation together.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Lean vs Six Sigma
Two approaches with different strengths.
Lean targets waste and lead time using tools like VSM, 5S and kanban. Six Sigma targets variation and defects using data and statistics through DMAIC. Choose by the type of problem.
Waste problem? Lean. Variation problem? Six Sigma.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Variation Basics
No two outputs are exactly the same.

Variation is the natural difference between outputs of the same process. Common-cause variation is built into the process; special-cause variation comes from a specific, unusual event and should be investigated.
Know which variation you are looking at before acting.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Process Capability
Can the process meet the specification every time?
Process capability compares the natural spread of a stable process with the specification limits. Indices such as Cp and Cpk express how well the process fits within the limits and how centred it is.
A process must be stable before capability means anything.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Defects per Unit
Average number of defects found per unit.
Defects per unit (DPU) is the total number of defects found divided by the number of units inspected. One unit can have more than one defect.
Count every defect, not just defective units.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
DPMO
Defects per million opportunities.

DPMO expresses defects relative to the number of opportunities for a defect. DPMO = defects ÷ (units × opportunities per unit) × 1,000,000. It allows comparison of processes with different complexity.
Define the opportunities clearly before calculating.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Yield
How many units come out right.

Yield is the proportion of units that pass a process step without defects. First-pass yield counts only units right the first time; rolled throughput yield multiplies first-pass yields across all steps.
Small losses at each step multiply across the process.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Sigma Level Concept
A common scale for process performance.

Sigma level is a way to express how many standard deviations fit between the process mean and the nearest specification limit. A higher sigma level means fewer defects; it is a summary, not the goal itself.
Higher sigma, fewer defects, but keep the customer measure in view.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
DMAIC Overview
Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control.

DMAIC is the five-phase Six Sigma method for improving an existing process: Define the problem, Measure the current performance, Analyze causes, Improve with tested solutions, and Control to sustain the gain.
Follow the phases; do not skip to solutions.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Define Phase
Agree the problem, scope and goal first.
The Define phase clarifies the problem, the customer and their requirements, the project scope, the goal and the team. Key outputs are a project charter, a SIPOC and the voice of the customer.
A well-defined problem is half solved.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Voice of Customer
What the customer says they need, in their words.

Voice of the Customer (VOC) is the collection of customer needs, expectations and complaints, gathered through interviews, surveys, complaints and feedback, and translated into measurable requirements.
Listen first, then translate into measures.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
CTQ Tree
From a broad need to measurable requirements.
A CTQ (critical-to-quality) tree breaks a broad customer need into specific drivers and then into measurable requirements with targets or limits.
Every CTQ must be measurable.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
SIPOC
Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers.
SIPOC is a high-level map of a process that lists Suppliers, Inputs, the main Process steps, Outputs and Customers. It sets the project boundaries and shows who is involved.
Agree the boundaries before diving into details.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Project Charter
The agreement that launches a project.
A project charter documents the business case, problem statement, goal, scope, team, timeline and sponsor. It aligns the team and management before work begins.
No charter, no shared direction.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Measure Phase
Understand current performance with reliable data.
The Measure phase establishes how the process performs today. The team defines measures, checks that the measurement system is reliable, collects baseline data and maps the process in detail.
Trust the measurement before you trust the data.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Operational Definition
Everyone measures the same thing the same way.
An operational definition describes exactly what to measure and how, including the method, the unit, the conditions and what counts as a defect, so that different people get the same result.
Define it so two people get the same answer.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Data Collection Plan
Plan what, how, when and who before collecting.
A data collection plan specifies what data to collect, the operational definitions, the sample size and frequency, who collects it, how it is recorded and how it will be used.
Plan the data before you collect it.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Measurement System
Is the measurement itself reliable?
A measurement system analysis (MSA) checks how much of the observed variation comes from the measurement system itself, through studies of repeatability, reproducibility, bias and stability.
Fix the gauge before blaming the process.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Analyze Phase
Find and verify the causes that drive the problem.
The Analyze phase identifies possible causes, then uses data and tests to verify which ones actually drive the problem. Tools include fishbone, 5 Whys, Pareto, scatter plots and hypothesis tests.
Verify causes with data before improving.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Cause-and-Effect Matrix
Score which inputs matter most to the CTQs.
A cause-and-effect (C&E) matrix rates how strongly each process input affects each customer requirement, weighted by importance, to prioritize which inputs to study first.
Prioritize inputs by impact on what the customer needs.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Improve Phase
Develop, test and prove solutions.
The Improve phase generates solutions for the verified root causes, selects the best ones, tests them in a pilot and confirms with data that the problem is reduced.
Pilot first, then scale what works.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Solution Selection
Choose solutions with clear criteria.
Solution selection compares options against agreed criteria, such as effect on the root cause, cost, time, risk and ease of implementation, often using a simple weighted matrix.
Decide with criteria, not with opinions.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Pilot Run
Test on a small scale before full rollout.
A pilot run tests a solution under real conditions on a limited scale, such as one line or one shift, to confirm it works, find side effects and refine it before full implementation.
Small pilots prevent big mistakes.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Control Phase
Hold the gain after the project ends.
The Control phase makes sure improvements last, using standard work, control plans, control charts, mistake-proofing and clear ownership, before the project is handed over to the process owner.
If it is not controlled, it will drift back.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Control Plan
One document for how the process stays in control.
A control plan lists, for each key process step, what is measured, the specification, the method, the sample size and frequency, who checks it and the reaction plan if it goes out of limits.
Every check needs a reaction plan.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Control Charts Intro
See whether variation is normal or special.
A control chart plots data over time with a centre line and control limits calculated from the process itself. Points outside the limits or unusual patterns signal special causes to investigate.
React to signals, not to every point.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Six Sigma Roles
Who does what in a Six Sigma program.

Six Sigma programs define roles: a Champion or sponsor removes barriers, Master Black Belts coach, Black Belts lead complex projects, Green Belts lead smaller projects, and team members contribute process knowledge.
Clear roles make projects move.
Six Sigma & DMAIC
Green Belt vs Black Belt
Two levels of Six Sigma practitioner.

Green Belts usually lead smaller projects part-time within their own area. Black Belts typically lead larger, cross-functional projects, use more advanced statistics and coach Green Belts. Exact requirements vary by training body.
Choose the level that matches the project scope.

Quality Tools
What Is Quality?
Meeting customer requirements, every time.
Quality means meeting customer and product requirements consistently. It is built into the process through good design, standards and control, not added by inspection at the end.
Build quality in; do not inspect it in.
Quality Tools
Cost of Poor Quality
The hidden cost of getting it wrong.
Cost of poor quality (COPQ) is the cost of not doing things right first time: internal failures (scrap, rework), external failures (complaints, returns), and appraisal and prevention costs.
Most quality costs are invisible until you list them.
Quality Tools
7 QC Tools
Seven simple tools that solve most problems.

The 7 basic quality tools are check sheet, histogram, Pareto chart, cause-and-effect diagram, scatter diagram, control chart and stratification (some lists include the flowchart). They help collect, display and analyze data.
Simple tools, used well, solve most problems.
Quality Tools
Check Sheet
Collect data simply, at the source.
A check sheet is a simple form for recording data as it happens, usually with tally marks by category, time or location. It makes patterns visible and data easy to summarize.
Easy to fill means more reliable data.
Quality Tools
Histogram
See the shape of your data.
A histogram is a bar chart showing how often values fall into ranges. It reveals the centre, spread and shape of the data, and whether it fits within specification limits.
Look at the shape before the average.
Quality Tools
Control Chart
A time-ordered view with limits from the process.
A control chart shows data in time order with a centre line and upper and lower control limits calculated from the process. It separates common-cause variation from special causes that need action.
Control limits come from the process, not the spec.
Quality Tools
Scatter Diagram
Is there a relationship between two variables?
A scatter diagram plots pairs of values to show whether two variables are related, and how strongly. A pattern suggests correlation, which still needs to be confirmed as cause.
Correlation is a clue, not proof of cause.
Quality Tools
Stratification
Split the data to reveal hidden patterns.
Stratification separates data into groups, such as by shift, machine, operator, material lot or product, to see whether a problem is concentrated in one group.
Split the data before drawing conclusions.
Quality Tools
Run Chart
Watch performance change over time.
A run chart plots data in time order, often with a median line. It shows trends, shifts and cycles, and is a simple first step before a control chart.
Plot it over time before judging a change.
Quality Tools
Pareto Chart
Rank problems to focus on the vital few.
A Pareto chart shows categories as bars in descending order with a cumulative percentage line. It highlights the few categories that account for most of the problem.
Start with the tallest bar.
Quality Tools
Process Flowchart
Draw the process to understand it.
A process flowchart shows the steps, decisions and flow of a process using standard symbols. It helps teams agree how the process actually works and spot unnecessary steps or loops.
Map the process as it really is, not as it should be.
Quality Tools
Inspection vs Prevention
Find defects late, or stop them from happening.
Inspection detects defects after they are made. Prevention stops defects from being made, through robust process design, standards, error-proofing and control at the source.
Prevention costs less than detection.
Quality Tools
First Pass Yield
Good units on the first try.
First pass yield (FPY) is the percentage of units that complete a process step correctly the first time, without rework, repair or re-inspection.
Rework hides in yields that ignore the first pass.
Quality Tools
Right First Time
Do it right the first time.
Right first time (RFT) means completing a task or product correctly on the first attempt, with no corrections. It applies to products, documents, batch records and changeovers.
Getting it right once is faster than fixing it twice.
Quality Tools
Defect Classification
Not all defects are equally serious.
Defect classification groups defects by severity, commonly critical (safety or legal risk), major (affects function or customer use) and minor (cosmetic). It guides sampling, reaction and priority.
Match the reaction to the severity.
Quality Tools
Sampling Basics
Check a part to judge the whole.
Sampling means inspecting a selected portion of a lot to make a decision about the whole lot. Good sampling is random, representative and follows a defined plan for sample size and acceptance.
A sample is only useful if it is random and planned.
Quality Tools
Acceptance Criteria
Know exactly what 'good' looks like.
Acceptance criteria are the defined conditions a product, material or task must meet to be accepted, such as specification limits, visual standards and test results.
If 'good' is not defined, it cannot be checked.
Quality Tools
Quality at Source
Each step owns the quality of its output.
Quality at source means each person and process step checks and guarantees the quality of its own work before passing it on, rather than relying on inspection downstream.
Do not pass a defect to the next step.
Quality Tools
Poka-Yoke
Make mistakes impossible, or instantly visible.
Poka-yoke (error-proofing) is a design feature or device that prevents a mistake from happening or makes it immediately obvious, so a defect is not produced or passed on.
Design the process so it is hard to get wrong.
Quality Tools
Error-Proofing Types
Prevent, detect, or warn.

Error-proofing devices are grouped by function: control (prevent the error or stop the process) and warning (signal the error). They can work by contact, by fixed value (count) or by motion step (sequence).
Prefer control devices over warnings where possible.
Quality Tools
Layered Process Audit
Short, frequent checks by every level of leadership.
A layered process audit (LPA) is a series of short audits of key process steps, done frequently by people at different levels, from supervisors to managers, to confirm standards are followed.
Many short checks beat one long audit.
Quality Tools
Quality Alert
Tell everyone about a quality risk, fast.
A quality alert is a short, visual notice that communicates a specific quality issue, what to look for and what to do, to everyone affected, while the problem is being solved.
Clear, visual and posted where the work happens.
Quality Tools
Nonconformance Report
Record what did not meet requirements.
A nonconformance report (NCR) documents a product, material or process that does not meet requirements: what was found, where, how much, immediate actions and disposition decisions.
Record it clearly so it can be fixed properly.
Quality Tools
CAPA
Corrective and preventive action.
CAPA is a structured system to investigate problems, find root causes, implement corrective actions to prevent recurrence and preventive actions to avoid similar problems, and check effectiveness.
Close a CAPA only after effectiveness is verified.
Quality Tools
8D Overview
Eight disciplines for solving serious problems.

8D is a team-based method for solving problems, often customer complaints: D1 team, D2 describe, D3 contain, D4 root cause, D5 choose actions, D6 implement and verify, D7 prevent recurrence, D8 recognize the team.
Contain fast, solve properly, prevent recurrence.
Quality Tools
8D D1-D3
Team, problem description and containment.
In 8D, D1 forms a cross-functional team, D2 describes the problem with facts (what, where, when, how many), and D3 puts interim containment in place to protect the customer.
Protect the customer before searching for the cause.
Quality Tools
8D D4-D5
Find the root cause and choose actions.
In 8D, D4 identifies and verifies the root cause of the problem and of why it was not detected. D5 selects permanent corrective actions and confirms they will address the cause.
Find why it happened and why it escaped.
Quality Tools
8D D6-D8
Implement, prevent recurrence, recognize.
In 8D, D6 implements the permanent actions and verifies their effectiveness, D7 prevents recurrence by updating systems and similar processes, and D8 closes the report and recognizes the team.
Fix it, prevent it everywhere, thank the team.
Quality Tools

A quality case study connects the problem, containment, root cause, countermeasure and verification. This example is illustrative; use your own data when presenting a real case.
Contain, find the cause, error-proof, verify.
Quality Tools

This month covered quality tools: define what good looks like, collect data with simple tools, find the vital few causes, prevent defects at the source and solve serious problems with CAPA and 8D.

TPM & Maintenance
What Is TPM?
Everyone takes care of the equipment.
Total Productive Maintenance (TPM) is a system for maximizing equipment effectiveness by involving everyone, from operators to managers, in preventing breakdowns, defects and accidents.
Equipment care is everyone's job.
TPM & Maintenance
TPM Pillars
The pillars that hold up TPM.

TPM is often described with pillars: autonomous maintenance, planned maintenance, focused improvement, quality maintenance, early equipment management, training, safety and environment, and TPM in offices, built on a 5S foundation.
Build on 5S, then raise the pillars.
TPM & Maintenance
OEE Overview
How much of the planned time is truly productive.
Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) measures how well equipment is used during planned production time. OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality.
OEE shows where the losses are, not who to blame.
TPM & Maintenance
Availability
Was the machine running when it should be?
Availability is the share of planned production time that the equipment actually runs. It is reduced by downtime such as breakdowns, changeovers and waiting for material.
Every unplanned stop reduces availability.
TPM & Maintenance
Performance
Did it run as fast as it should?
Performance compares actual output with what the equipment could produce at its ideal cycle time during run time. It is reduced by slow running and minor stops.
Small stops and slow speed hide here.
TPM & Maintenance
Quality Rate
How much of the output was good?
The quality rate in OEE is good units divided by total units produced. It is reduced by scrap, rework and start-up rejects.
Count rework as a loss, not as good output.
TPM & Maintenance
OEE Calculation
Put the three factors together.
OEE is calculated by multiplying availability, performance and quality. Each factor is a percentage of the ideal, so OEE shows overall effectiveness in one number.
Improve the factor with the biggest loss first.
TPM & Maintenance
Six Big Losses
The losses that reduce equipment effectiveness.
The six big losses are breakdowns, setup and adjustments (availability losses), minor stops and reduced speed (performance losses), and start-up rejects and production rejects (quality losses).
Name the loss before trying to fix it.
TPM & Maintenance
Autonomous Maintenance
Operators care for their own equipment.
Autonomous maintenance gives operators responsibility for basic equipment care: cleaning, inspection, lubrication, tightening and early detection of abnormalities, following clear standards.
Operators are the first line of equipment care.
TPM & Maintenance
Initial Cleaning
Clean to find hidden problems.

Initial cleaning is the first step of autonomous maintenance: a thorough cleaning of the equipment that restores it to basic condition and reveals hidden defects such as leaks, cracks and loose parts.
Every tag found during cleaning is a future breakdown avoided.
TPM & Maintenance
Inspection Standards
Define what to check, how and how often.
Inspection standards list each check point on the equipment, the method, the normal condition, the frequency and who does it, often with photos, so checks are consistent.
Make normal visible so abnormal is obvious.
TPM & Maintenance
Lubrication Basics
The right lubricant, amount and time.
Lubrication basics cover using the correct lubricant, in the correct amount, at the correct point and interval, and keeping lubricants clean and clearly labelled.
Right lubricant, right point, right amount, right time.
TPM & Maintenance
Planned Maintenance
Maintenance scheduled before failure.
Planned maintenance is maintenance work scheduled in advance, based on time, usage or condition, to prevent failures and keep equipment in good condition.
Plan the stop before the machine plans it for you.
TPM & Maintenance
Preventive vs Predictive
Fixed intervals versus actual condition.
Preventive maintenance is done at fixed intervals of time or usage. Predictive maintenance uses condition data, such as vibration, temperature or oil analysis, to decide when maintenance is needed.
Use condition data where failures give warning signs.
TPM & Maintenance
Breakdown Maintenance
Run to failure, then repair.
Breakdown maintenance means repairing equipment after it fails. It can be acceptable for low-cost, non-critical items, but for critical equipment it causes unplanned downtime and risk.
Choose run-to-failure deliberately, not by default.
TPM & Maintenance
MTBF
Average time between failures.
Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) is the average running time between one failure and the next. A higher MTBF means more reliable equipment.
Track failures to see reliability improve.
TPM & Maintenance
MTTR
Average time to repair a failure.
Mean Time To Repair (MTTR) is the average time needed to restore equipment after a failure, including diagnosis, waiting for parts and repair. A lower MTTR means faster recovery.
Spares, skills and standards cut repair time.
TPM & Maintenance
Maintenance Backlog
Work waiting to be done.

Maintenance backlog is the amount of approved maintenance work not yet completed, often expressed in hours or weeks of available labour. A growing backlog signals that capacity or planning needs attention.
Watch the backlog trend, not just the size.
TPM & Maintenance
Criticality Analysis
Focus effort on the equipment that matters most.
Criticality analysis ranks equipment by the impact of its failure on safety, quality, delivery and cost, and by how likely failure is, to decide maintenance priorities and strategies.
Not all equipment deserves the same strategy.
TPM & Maintenance
Spare Parts Strategy
The right spares, in the right quantity.
A spare parts strategy decides which parts to stock, how many and where, based on equipment criticality, lead time, failure rate and cost, balancing availability against inventory.
Stock for criticality and lead time, not for comfort.
TPM & Maintenance
Failure Mode Basics
How a part fails, and what happens next.
A failure mode is the way a component or process can fail, such as wear, leakage, cracking or misalignment. Understanding failure modes, causes and effects helps plan prevention.
Know how it fails to know how to prevent it.
TPM & Maintenance
FMEA
Find and rank risks before they become failures.

Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) systematically lists possible failure modes, their effects and causes, rates severity, occurrence and detection, and prioritizes actions to reduce the highest risks.
Act on the highest risks before they occur.
TPM & Maintenance
Condition Monitoring
Listen to the machine before it fails.
Condition monitoring tracks indicators of equipment health, such as vibration, temperature, noise, oil condition or current, to detect developing problems early.
Trends warn you before breakdowns do.
TPM & Maintenance
Vibration Basics
Vibration tells the story of rotating equipment.
Vibration analysis measures the vibration of rotating equipment to detect problems such as imbalance, misalignment, looseness and bearing wear, often before they can be heard or felt.
Set a baseline, then watch the trend.
TPM & Maintenance
Thermography
See heat that signals trouble.
Thermography uses infrared cameras to show temperature differences on equipment. Hot spots can reveal loose electrical connections, overloaded circuits, failing bearings or insulation problems.
Hot spots are early warnings.
TPM & Maintenance
Maintenance Planning
Prepare the job before the technician starts.
Maintenance planning defines what work is needed, how to do it safely, which parts, tools, skills and permits are required, and how long it will take, before the job is scheduled.
A well-planned job is a faster, safer job.
TPM & Maintenance
Maintenance Scheduling
Put planned jobs on the calendar.
Maintenance scheduling assigns planned jobs to specific dates, times and people, coordinated with the production plan so equipment is available and work is done efficiently.
Schedule with production, not against it.
TPM & Maintenance

A TPM case study shows how a team applied autonomous and planned maintenance to one machine. This example is illustrative; use measured results from your own site.
Start on one machine, prove it, then expand.
TPM & Maintenance
OEE Improvement Example
Use OEE to find and fix the biggest loss.
An OEE improvement starts by breaking OEE into its factors and losses, picking the largest loss, finding its causes and fixing them, then tracking OEE to confirm the gain.
Break it down, pick the biggest loss, fix it.
TPM & Maintenance
