Care, measure and improve equipment together.
This month covered TPM: involve operators in daily care, plan maintenance before failure, measure OEE and its losses, use reliability measures like MTBF and MTTR, and focus on critical equipment.
Care daily, plan ahead, measure losses, improve.
Standard Work & Productivity
What Is Standard Work?
The current best way to do the job, written down.

Standard work documents the current best and safest method for a task, with three elements: the work sequence, the time to do it (against takt) and the standard work-in-process. It is the baseline for improvement.
No standard, no improvement.
Standard Work & Productivity
Takt Time
The pace the customer demands.
Takt time is the rate at which products must be completed to meet customer demand. Takt time = available production time ÷ customer demand for that period.
Takt is set by demand, not by the machine.
Standard Work & Productivity
Cycle Time
How long one cycle of the work takes.
Cycle time is the time it takes to complete one cycle of an operation or produce one unit at a process step, measured from start to start or end to end.
Measure cycle time at the process, not from the spreadsheet.
Standard Work & Productivity
Lead Time
The total time from start to finish.
Lead time is the total elapsed time from a request or order to delivery, or from material arrival to product shipment. It includes processing, waiting, inspection, movement and storage.
Customers feel lead time, not cycle time.
Standard Work & Productivity
Work Sequence
The order in which the work is done.
The work sequence is the defined order of steps an operator follows to complete a task safely and efficiently. A consistent sequence reduces variation in time and quality.
Same sequence, every time, by everyone.
Standard Work & Productivity
Standard WIP
The minimum work-in-process for smooth flow.
Standard WIP is the minimum amount of material that must be within a process, including units in machines, to keep the work flowing according to the standard sequence.
Too much WIP hides problems; too little stops flow.
Standard Work & Productivity
Line Balancing
Share the work evenly against takt.
Line balancing distributes work across stations so that each station's cycle time is close to, but not above, takt time. It reduces waiting at some stations and overload at others.
Balance the work to the pace of demand.
Standard Work & Productivity
Yamazumi Chart
A stacked chart of work content per operator.
A Yamazumi chart shows each operator's or station's work as stacked blocks of tasks, compared with a takt line. It makes imbalance and non-value-added work easy to see.
See the imbalance, then rebalance the tasks.
Standard Work & Productivity
Bottleneck
The step that limits the whole process.
A bottleneck is the process step with the lowest capacity relative to demand. It sets the output of the whole system; improving other steps does not increase output.
An hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost for the whole line.
Standard Work & Productivity
Theory of Constraints
Manage the system through its constraint.
The Theory of Constraints (TOC) says every system has at least one constraint that limits its output. Its five focusing steps are: identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, and repeat.
Improve the constraint first; everything else follows.
Standard Work & Productivity
Constraint Management
Keep the constraint running, always.
Constraint management means protecting the constraint's time: keep a buffer in front of it, prevent its stoppages, check quality before it, and run it through breaks and changeovers where possible.
Protect every minute of the constraint.
Standard Work & Productivity
Capacity vs Demand
Can we make what customers want?
Capacity is the maximum output a process can produce in a period. Comparing capacity with demand shows whether the plant can meet orders, has spare capacity or must add shifts, improve OEE or invest.
Know your real capacity, not the nameplate.
Standard Work & Productivity
Productivity vs Utilization
Busy is not the same as productive.
Productivity is useful output per unit of input. Utilization is how much of the available time a resource is busy. High utilization of a non-constraint can create excess inventory without more sales.
Measure output that customers need, not activity.
Standard Work & Productivity
Man-Machine Chart
See how people and machines share time.
A man-machine chart shows, on a timeline, when the operator and the machine are working, waiting or idle. It helps find waiting time and better ways to combine tasks.
Use machine time to do useful operator work.
Standard Work & Productivity
Spaghetti Diagram
Draw the walking paths to see wasted motion.
A spaghetti diagram traces the actual path of a person or material through the work area on a layout drawing. Long, crossing paths reveal motion and transport waste.
If the lines look like spaghetti, the layout needs work.
Standard Work & Productivity
Work Combination Table
Combine manual work, machine time and walking.
A standard work combination table shows each step's manual time, machine time and walking time on a timeline against takt, so the work can be arranged to fit within takt.
Fit manual, machine and walking time inside takt.
Standard Work & Productivity
Time Study
Measure how long the work really takes.
A time study observes and times a task over several cycles, breaks it into elements, and records the repeatable time for each element, along with any irregular events.
Observe several cycles; record what really happens.
Standard Work & Productivity
Motion Economy
Make every movement easier and shorter.
Principles of motion economy aim to reduce effort and time: keep items within easy reach, use both hands, avoid unnecessary movements, use gravity feeds and design comfortable work heights.
Short, easy, natural movements.
Standard Work & Productivity
Ergonomics Basics
Fit the work to the person.
Ergonomics designs tasks, workstations and tools to fit people's capabilities, reducing strain from lifting, awkward postures, repetition and force.
Good ergonomics is good productivity.
Standard Work & Productivity
SMED Overview
Single-Minute Exchange of Die: faster changeovers.
SMED is a method for reducing changeover time by separating internal setup (done while stopped) from external setup (done while running), converting internal to external, and streamlining both.
Do as much as possible while the machine is still running.
Standard Work & Productivity
Internal vs External Setup
What must happen while stopped, and what need not.
Internal setup tasks can only be done while the machine is stopped, such as changing a nozzle. External setup tasks can be done while it is running, such as fetching parts, tools and documents.
Move every possible task outside the stop.
Standard Work & Productivity
Setup Reduction
Shorten every step of the changeover.
Setup reduction streamlines changeovers by using quick-release fasteners, standard heights and positions, pre-set tools, parallel work by two people and eliminating adjustments.
Eliminate adjustments; set it right first time.
Standard Work & Productivity
Changeover Checklist
Everything ready before the line stops.
A changeover checklist lists the parts, tools, materials, documents and people needed, and the steps in order, so nothing is missing when the changeover starts.
Check before you stop, not after.
Standard Work & Productivity
Production Pitch
A regular interval to check output against plan.
Pitch is a set time interval, often a multiple of takt that matches a standard pack quantity, used to release work and check whether production is on schedule throughout the shift.
Check progress at every pitch, not just at shift end.
Standard Work & Productivity
Daily Production Control
Know every hour if you are on plan.
Daily production control tracks planned versus actual output at regular intervals during the shift, records reasons for gaps and triggers quick responses, usually on an hour-by-hour board.
React during the shift, not the next day.
Standard Work & Productivity
Standard Work Audit
Check that the standard is followed and still right.
A standard work audit observes whether the work is done according to the standard and whether the standard is still the best method. Gaps lead to coaching or to updating the standard.
Audit to learn, then update or coach.
Standard Work & Productivity
Productivity Case Study
An illustrative productivity improvement.
A productivity case study shows how a team improved good output per resource used. This example is illustrative; use measured data from your own process.
Balance, simplify, track, then verify.
Standard Work & Productivity
Bottleneck Case Study
An illustrative bottleneck story.
A bottleneck case study shows how finding and protecting the constraint increased system output. This example is illustrative; use your own data in a real case.
Find the constraint, protect it, then improve it.
Standard Work & Productivity
Standard Work Review
Sequence, time and WIP, against takt.
Standard work review: document the best current method with a clear sequence, cycle time compared with takt and standard WIP; audit it regularly; and update it when an improvement is proven.
The standard is the base; improvement builds on it.
Standard Work & Productivity
Productivity Review
Productivity tools from takt to SMED.
Productivity review: match work to takt, balance the line, find and protect the bottleneck, reduce changeovers with SMED, remove motion waste and track output during the shift.
Pace, balance, constraint, changeover, control.
VSM & Flow
What Is Value Stream Mapping?
See the whole flow of material and information.
Value stream mapping (VSM) is a visual method for drawing all the steps, material flows and information flows needed to deliver a product, with key data, to find waste and plan a better future state.
Map the whole stream before improving any part.
VSM & Flow
Current State Map
Draw the stream as it really is today.
A current state map shows how the value stream works now, based on direct observation: process steps, data boxes, inventory, information flows and a timeline of lead time versus processing time.
Walk it and draw it as it is, not as it should be.
VSM & Flow
Future State Map
Design how the stream should flow.

A future state map shows how the value stream should work after improvement, using Lean principles: produce to takt, create flow where possible, use pull where flow is not possible, and schedule at one point.
Design the future, then plan the steps to get there.
VSM & Flow
Information Flow
How each step knows what to do next.
Information flow shows how orders, forecasts and schedules move from the customer through planning to each process. Complicated or multiple schedules often cause overproduction and confusion.
Simplify the information, and the material will follow.
VSM & Flow
Material Flow
How material moves between steps.
Material flow shows how materials move through the value stream: pushed to the next step, flowing continuously, or pulled from a supermarket. It also shows where inventory accumulates.
Where material waits, lead time grows.
VSM & Flow
Process Data Box
The key facts for each process step.
A process data box records key data under each step on a value stream map, such as cycle time, changeover time, uptime, number of operators, batch size and shifts.
Collect data at the process, not from old reports.
VSM & Flow
Timeline Calculation
Add up waiting and processing along the stream.
The VSM timeline shows, step by step, the waiting time (often estimated from inventory ÷ daily demand) and the processing time. Totals give lead time and processing time.
Inventory divided by demand gives waiting time.
VSM & Flow
VA vs NVA Time
How much of the time actually adds value?
On a value stream, value-added (VA) time is the time when the product is transformed in a way the customer pays for. Non-value-added (NVA) time is everything else. The VA share is often very small.
Shrink the waiting, not just the work.
VSM & Flow
Value Stream Lead Time
From raw material to the customer's hands.
Value stream lead time is the total time a product takes to move through the whole stream, including all waiting and storage. It is the time the customer and the business actually experience.
Lower inventory between steps to cut lead time.
VSM & Flow
Takt-Based Flow
Set the pace of the stream by demand.
Takt-based flow means designing the value stream so the pacemaker process runs at takt time and other steps support that pace, avoiding overproduction and starvation.
One pace for the whole stream: takt.
VSM & Flow
Continuous Flow
Move product without stopping between steps.
Continuous flow means producing and moving one item, or a small batch, at a time through a series of steps, with each step doing only what the next one needs.
Flow where you can; pull where you cannot.
VSM & Flow
One-Piece Flow
Make and move one piece at a time.
One-piece flow means each unit moves to the next step as soon as it is complete. It shortens lead time, exposes defects immediately and reduces WIP, but needs balanced, reliable steps.
Smaller batches, faster feedback.
VSM & Flow
Batch Size
Smaller batches, shorter lead time.
Batch size is the number of units processed together before moving on. Large batches increase waiting and inventory; reducing batch size usually needs shorter changeovers.
Reduce changeover time to reduce batch size.
VSM & Flow
FIFO Lane
First in, first out, with a limit.
A FIFO lane is a controlled queue between two processes that holds a maximum quantity in sequence. When it is full, the upstream process stops, preventing overproduction.
Fixed order, fixed limit.
VSM & Flow
Supermarket Pull
Replenish only what was taken.
A supermarket is a controlled store of parts or products between processes. The downstream process takes what it needs, and the upstream process replenishes only what was taken.
Take what you need; replace what was taken.
VSM & Flow
Kanban Basics
A signal to produce or move.
Kanban is a signalling system, using cards, bins or electronic signals, that authorizes production or movement of a set quantity when the downstream process uses material.
No signal, no production.
VSM & Flow
Kanban Card
What a kanban card must tell you.
A kanban card carries the information needed to act: item name and code, quantity, supplier process or location, customer process or location, and card number.
Clear cards prevent wrong refills.
VSM & Flow
WIP Limits
Cap the work in progress to keep it flowing.
A WIP limit sets the maximum number of items allowed in a process step or queue. When the limit is reached, no new work starts until something finishes, which exposes bottlenecks.
Stop starting; start finishing.
VSM & Flow
Heijunka
Level the mix and volume of production.
Heijunka is production levelling: spreading the volume and mix of products evenly over time instead of producing large batches of one product, so the upstream flow is steady.
Level the schedule to steady the flow.
VSM & Flow
Production Leveling
Even out the daily load.
Production levelling smooths the total volume produced each day or shift, so people, machines and suppliers see a steady workload rather than peaks and troughs.
Steady load, steady quality.
VSM & Flow
Pacemaker Process
The one step that sets the pace.
The pacemaker process is the single point in the value stream that receives the schedule. Steps upstream are replenished by pull; steps downstream follow in flow.
Schedule one point, not every point.
VSM & Flow
Milk Run
A fixed route that delivers regularly.
A milk run is a fixed route and schedule for delivering materials to several points or collecting from several suppliers, in small, frequent quantities.
Fixed route, fixed time, small loads.
VSM & Flow
Layout Optimization
Arrange the space to suit the flow.
Layout optimization arranges equipment, storage and workstations so materials and people travel the shortest, safest path in the order of the process, with clear aisles and access.
Let the process sequence shape the layout.
VSM & Flow
Cellular Manufacturing
Group steps into a compact cell.
Cellular manufacturing groups the machines and people needed for a product family into a compact cell, often U-shaped, so work flows step to step with minimal transport and WIP.
Bring the steps together; let the product flow.
VSM & Flow
Flow Interruptions
What stops the flow, and how to find it.
Flow interruptions are events that stop or slow product movement: breakdowns, missing material, quality holds, changeovers, waiting for approval and imbalance between steps.
Log every interruption; fix the most frequent.
VSM & Flow
VSM Common Mistakes
Traps that make maps less useful.
Common VSM mistakes include mapping from the office, mapping too many products at once, skipping information flow, using old data and creating a future state without an action plan.
Map from the floor, then act on the map.
VSM & Flow
VSM Case Study
An illustrative value stream improvement.
A VSM case study shows the current state, the future state design and the actions taken. This example is illustrative; use your own measured data for real cases.
Current state, future state, action plan, review.
VSM & Flow
Future State Actions
Turn the future state into a plan.
Future state actions are the specific projects, owners and dates needed to move from the current to the future state, often grouped into loops and reviewed regularly.
A future state without owners is just a drawing.
VSM & Flow
Flow Metrics
Measure how well work flows.
Flow metrics show how smoothly work moves: lead time, WIP, throughput, VA ratio and on-time delivery. Tracked together, they show whether flow improvements are working.
Track lead time and WIP together.
VSM & Flow
VSM Review
See the stream, design the flow, pull the rest.
VSM and flow review: map the current state from the floor, design a future state with takt, flow, pull and levelling, create an action plan with owners, and measure lead time and WIP.
Map, design, act, measure, repeat.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Safety as a Lean Foundation
No improvement is worth an injury.
Safety is the foundation of Lean: a stable, organized and standardized workplace is also a safer one. Every improvement should be checked for its effect on safety before it is adopted.
Safety first in every change.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Near Miss Reporting
Report the event that almost happened.
A near miss is an unplanned event that could have caused injury, illness or damage but did not. Reporting near misses lets teams fix hazards before someone is hurt.
Every near miss is a free lesson.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Hazard vs Risk
Something that can harm, versus how likely and how bad.
A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm, such as a chemical, a moving part or a height. Risk combines how likely harm is to happen and how severe it would be.
Control the hazard to lower the risk.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Risk Assessment
Identify, evaluate and control risks before work.
A risk assessment identifies hazards in a task, evaluates the risk, decides on controls, records the result and reviews it when the task or conditions change.
Assess before you act; review when things change.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Hierarchy of Controls
Start with the most effective control.
The hierarchy of controls ranks risk controls from most to least effective: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls and personal protective equipment (PPE).
PPE is the last line of defence, not the first.
Safety & EHS Excellence
5S for Safety
An organized workplace is a safer workplace.
5S supports safety by removing trip hazards, keeping exits and emergency equipment clear, marking hazardous zones, and making unsafe conditions easy to see.
Clutter hides hazards; order reveals them.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Unsafe Condition vs Act
Fix the condition and understand the behaviour.
An unsafe condition is a hazard in the workplace, such as a missing guard or a wet floor. An unsafe act is a behaviour that increases risk, such as bypassing a guard. Most incidents involve both.
Ask why the unsafe act made sense to the person.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Permit to Work Basics
Authorize high-risk work in a controlled way.

A permit-to-work system controls high-risk, non-routine tasks, such as hot work, confined space entry or work at height, by defining the hazards, controls, isolations and authorizations before work starts.
No permit, no high-risk work.
Safety & EHS Excellence
LOTO Overview
Lock out, tag out, verify zero energy.
Lockout/tagout (LOTO) is a procedure to isolate all energy sources, such as electrical, mechanical, pneumatic and hydraulic, apply personal locks and tags, and verify zero energy before maintenance.
Try to start it before you touch it.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Machine Guarding
Keep people away from moving parts.
Machine guarding prevents contact with dangerous moving parts using fixed guards, interlocked guards, light curtains and other devices. Guards must not be easy to bypass.
If a guard is bypassed, ask why and fix that.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Chemical Compatibility
Some chemicals must never meet.
Chemical compatibility means knowing which substances can react dangerously when mixed or stored together, such as acids with bases or oxidizers with flammables, and segregating them accordingly.
Check the SDS before you store or mix.
Safety & EHS Excellence
SDS Essentials
The first place to look for chemical hazards.

A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) provides key information on a chemical: hazards, composition, first aid, firefighting, handling and storage, exposure controls, PPE and disposal, in a standard section format.
Read the SDS before you handle it.
Safety & EHS Excellence
PPE Selection
The right protection for the specific hazard.

PPE selection starts from the risk assessment and the SDS: choose equipment that protects against the specific hazard, fits the user, is compatible with other PPE, and is maintained and worn correctly.
Match the PPE to the hazard, not to habit.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Emergency Preparedness
Know what to do before it happens.
Emergency preparedness means planning and practising the response to events such as fire, chemical spills, injuries and power failures: roles, alarms, routes, assembly points, equipment and drills.
Practise the plan before you need it.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Fire Safety Basics
Remove one side of the fire triangle.
Fire needs fuel, heat (an ignition source) and oxygen. Fire safety controls these by managing flammable materials, controlling ignition sources, and providing detection, suppression and escape.
Control fuel and ignition before a fire starts.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Ergonomics & Safety
Prevent strain injuries by design.
Ergonomics in safety reduces musculoskeletal injuries by limiting heavy lifting, repetitive movements, awkward postures and forceful exertions through workplace and task design.
Design out the strain, do not just train it out.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Safety Observation
Watch, talk and learn about safe work.
A safety observation is a short, structured observation of a task, followed by a respectful conversation about what was done safely and what could be safer.
Observe to learn, not to catch people out.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Behavior-Based Safety
Understand and improve everyday safety behaviour.
Behaviour-based safety focuses on observing, discussing and reinforcing safe behaviours, while also addressing the systems and conditions that influence those behaviours.
Fix the system that shapes the behaviour.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Safety Kaizen
Small improvements that remove hazards.
A safety kaizen is a small, quick improvement that reduces a specific hazard, made by the people doing the work, often after a near miss or observation.
See a hazard, fix it small and fast.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Incident Investigation
Learn from what happened to stop it happening again.
Incident investigation gathers facts about an event, establishes the sequence, identifies immediate and underlying causes, and agrees actions to prevent recurrence, without blaming individuals.
Investigate to learn, not to blame.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Root Cause of Incidents
Look beyond the person to the system.
Root cause analysis of incidents asks why the conditions and behaviours existed, looking at design, procedures, training, supervision and culture, so actions address underlying causes.
'Human error' is where the investigation starts.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Safety KPI Basics
Measure safety ahead of and after the event.

Safety KPIs include lagging indicators, such as injury rates, which measure outcomes, and leading indicators, such as near-miss reports, observations and actions closed, which measure prevention activity.
Lead with prevention measures; learn from outcome measures.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Safety Walk
Go and see safety where the work is done.
A safety walk is a planned visit by leaders to the workplace to observe conditions and work practices, talk with employees about risks, and follow up on actions.
Ask, listen and follow up.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Contractor Safety
Same standards for everyone on site.
Contractor safety ensures that contractors are selected for competence, briefed on site hazards and rules, work under the right permits, are supervised, and are included in incident reporting.
Contractors get the same protection as employees.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Safety Training Matrix
Who is trained in what, at a glance.
A safety training matrix lists each person against the safety training they need, such as LOTO, forklift, chemical handling and first aid, showing status and refresher due dates.
No training, no task.
Safety & EHS Excellence
EHS Visual Management
Make safety status visible to everyone.
EHS visual management displays safety and environmental information at the workplace: hazard signs, PPE zones, emergency equipment locations, safety cross calendars and open actions.
If safety is visible, it is talked about.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Safety Case Study
An illustrative safety improvement story.
A safety case study shows the hazard, how it was found, the controls chosen using the hierarchy of controls, and how effectiveness was checked. This example is illustrative.
Use the hierarchy, then verify the control works.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Risk Reduction Prioritization
Tackle the biggest risks first.
Risk reduction prioritization ranks risks by severity and likelihood, then applies the most effective practical controls first to the highest risks, while keeping track of the rest.
Highest risk first, strongest control first.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Safety Review
Hazards, controls, people and culture.
Safety review: identify hazards, assess risk, apply the hierarchy of controls, control energy and chemicals, prepare for emergencies, learn from near misses and incidents, and lead visibly.
Identify, control, learn, lead.
Safety & EHS Excellence
Safety Culture
How people think and act about safety when no one is watching.

Safety culture is the shared values, beliefs and behaviours about safety in an organization. A strong culture shows in open reporting, leaders who listen, and everyone feeling able to stop unsafe work.
Anyone can stop unsafe work, and is thanked for it.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Inventory Fundamentals
Stock that serves flow, not stock that hides problems.
Inventory is material held for future use or sale: raw materials, work in progress and finished goods. It protects against variation, but too much ties up cash and space and hides problems.
Hold enough to protect flow, no more.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Raw Material vs WIP vs FG
Three types of inventory along the stream.

Raw material is purchased input not yet used. Work in progress (WIP) is partly processed material. Finished goods (FG) are completed products ready for sale. Each type has different causes and controls.
Know which type of stock is growing, and why.
Supply Chain & Inventory
ABC Analysis
Focus control on the items that matter most by value.

ABC analysis classifies inventory items by their share of annual consumption value: A items (few items, high value), B items (moderate) and C items (many items, low value), so control effort matches importance.
Tight control for A, simple control for C.
Supply Chain & Inventory
XYZ Analysis
Classify items by how predictable demand is.
XYZ analysis classifies items by demand variability: X items have steady demand, Y items vary somewhat, and Z items are irregular. Combined with ABC, it guides planning and stocking policy.
Steady demand: pull. Erratic demand: plan or make to order.
Supply Chain & Inventory
FIFO
Use the oldest stock first.
FIFO (first in, first out) means using or shipping material in the order it was received or made, so older stock does not age in the store.
Design the storage so FIFO happens naturally.
Supply Chain & Inventory
FEFO
Use the stock that expires first.
FEFO (first expired, first out) means issuing material with the earliest expiry date first, which matters for products and materials with a shelf life.
With shelf life, expiry date beats arrival date.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Reorder Point
When to order again.
The reorder point is the stock level at which a new order should be placed. A common form: reorder point = demand during lead time + safety stock.
Order when stock reaches the trigger, not when it runs out.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Safety Stock
A buffer for uncertainty.
Safety stock is extra inventory held to protect against variation in demand and supply lead time. Its size depends on how much variation exists and the service level wanted.
Reduce variation to reduce safety stock.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Economic Order Quantity
Balance ordering cost against holding cost.

Economic order quantity (EOQ) is a classic model for the order size that minimizes the total of ordering and holding costs under steady demand: EOQ = √(2 × annual demand × cost per order ÷ holding cost per unit per year).
Use EOQ as a guide, then apply real constraints.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Inventory Accuracy
System stock should match physical stock.
Inventory accuracy measures how closely the recorded inventory matches the actual physical quantity and location. Poor accuracy causes stockouts, excess orders and planning errors.
A plan is only as good as the stock record.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Cycle Counting
Count a little often instead of everything once.
Cycle counting counts a small portion of inventory on a regular schedule, often more frequently for A items, so errors are found and their causes fixed throughout the year.
Count often, fix the cause of every difference.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Stockout vs Overstock
Two opposite problems with one root: poor flow.
A stockout is when an item is not available when needed. Overstock is holding far more than needed. Both often come from poor forecasting, long lead times, large batches and inaccurate records.
Replenish by consumption to avoid both.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Supplier Quality
Good materials in, good products out.

Supplier quality means ensuring purchased materials meet requirements consistently, through clear specifications, supplier selection, incoming checks, performance monitoring and joint problem solving.
Specify clearly, measure regularly, improve together.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Supplier Lead Time
The time from order to receipt.
Supplier lead time is the time from placing an order to receiving the material. Its length and variability directly affect reorder points and safety stock.
Reliable lead time matters as much as short lead time.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Material Readiness
Everything ready before production starts.
Material readiness means confirming, before a production run, that all required materials are available in the right quantity, quality status and location.
Check readiness before the line is scheduled to start.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Shortage Management
Act early when material will run short.
Shortage management detects potential material shortages early, prioritizes the orders affected, and coordinates actions such as expediting, substitutions (where approved) or re-sequencing the plan.
See shortages days ahead, not at the line.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Warehouse Slotting
Put each item in the best location.
Warehouse slotting assigns storage locations based on how often items are picked, their size and weight, and safety needs, so picking is fast and safe.
Fast movers close and low.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Receiving Inspection
Check what arrives before it is used.
Receiving inspection checks incoming materials against the purchase order and specification: identity, quantity, condition, labelling, documents and, where required, sampling for testing.
Quarantine until released.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Packaging Material Control
The right label, carton and cap, every time.
Packaging material control ensures that printed and unprinted packaging materials are correct, approved, counted, stored securely and reconciled, to prevent mix-ups and mislabelling.
Count it out, count it back.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Batch Traceability
Trace every batch backward and forward.
Batch traceability means being able to trace a finished batch back to its materials, equipment and records, and forward to the customers who received it.
Record it at each step so you can trace it later.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Lot Control
Keep each lot identified and separate.
Lot control identifies each lot or batch of material or product and keeps it separated and labelled, so status, quality and use can be tracked and recalls limited.
Never mix lots without a record.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Dispatch Readiness
Everything checked before the truck leaves.
Dispatch readiness confirms that the order is complete, correctly labelled, documented and loaded safely before shipment.
Check the order before it leaves, not after a complaint.
Supply Chain & Inventory
OTIF
On time, in full: the customer's view of delivery.
OTIF measures the share of orders delivered on time and in full, as agreed with the customer. An order counts only if both conditions are met.
Late or short both count as a miss.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Forecast vs Demand
What we predicted versus what customers ordered.
A forecast is an estimate of future demand; actual demand is what customers order. Tracking forecast error helps improve planning and set the right stock buffers.
Measure forecast error to improve it.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Bullwhip Effect
Small changes at the customer, big swings upstream.
The bullwhip effect is the amplification of demand variability as orders move upstream in a supply chain, caused by batching, forecasting on orders rather than consumption, and delays.
Share real demand to calm the whip.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Kanban Replenishment
Replenish by consumption signals.
Kanban replenishment refills materials only when a signal shows they have been used, keeping stock within set limits and linking supply to actual consumption.
Use one bin, refill one bin.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Inventory Waste Case
An illustrative case of excess stock.
An inventory waste case shows how excess stock built up, what it cost and how it was reduced. This example is illustrative; use your own data for real cases.
Cheap to buy can be expensive to hold.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Warehouse 5S
An organized warehouse is safer and faster.
Warehouse 5S organizes storage areas with clear locations, labels, marked aisles, removed obsolete stock and regular cleaning, so picking is accurate and safe.
Every pallet has a home.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Supply Chain Case Study
An illustrative supply chain improvement.
A supply chain case study connects demand, planning, inventory and supplier performance. This example is illustrative; use your own data for real cases.
Fix the data and the agreement, then the flow follows.
Supply Chain & Inventory
Inventory Review
Right material, right place, right time.
Inventory review: know your stock types, classify with ABC and XYZ, use FIFO or FEFO, set reorder points and safety stock, keep records accurate, and measure delivery with OTIF.
Classify, control, count, deliver.
Leadership & Daily Management
Leader Standard Work
The routine that keeps leaders at the gemba.

Leader standard work is a defined routine of tasks for leaders at each level, such as board reviews, gemba walks, audits and coaching, with times and frequencies, so the management system runs consistently.
Leaders need standard work too.
Leadership & Daily Management
Daily Management System
A daily rhythm to see, solve and sustain.
A daily management system links visual boards, short tiered meetings, leader standard work and problem-solving so that performance gaps are seen and acted on every day.
See it daily, solve it daily.
Leadership & Daily Management
Tier Meetings
Short meetings that escalate issues fast.
Tier meetings are short, standing meetings held at successive levels, from team to department to plant, each reviewing performance and escalating issues that need help from the next level.
Short, standing, on time, with escalation.
Leadership & Daily Management
Visual KPI Board
Show performance where the work is done.
A visual KPI board displays a few key measures with targets, trends and status colours at the workplace, so the team can see performance and discuss actions.
Few measures, clear status, linked actions.
Leadership & Daily Management
SQDCP
Safety, Quality, Delivery, Cost, People.
SQDCP is a common structure for daily boards and meetings that reviews Safety, Quality, Delivery, Cost and People in that order, keeping attention on what matters most.
Start every review with safety.
Leadership & Daily Management
Escalation Process
Know who to call, and when.
An escalation process defines when a problem should be raised to the next level, how, and how quickly the next level must respond, so problems do not stay hidden or stuck.
Escalation rules turn waiting into action.
Leadership & Daily Management
Gemba Leadership
Lead from where the work happens.
Gemba leadership means leaders spend regular time at the workplace, observing processes, asking questions, supporting problem-solving and removing obstacles, rather than managing only from reports.
Ask, listen, help, follow up.
Leadership & Daily Management
Coaching at Gemba
Teach by asking, at the place of work.
Coaching at gemba helps people improve their own problem-solving by asking open questions about the target, the current condition, obstacles and the next step, instead of giving answers.
Ask the next question instead of giving the answer.
Leadership & Daily Management
Hoshin Kanri Intro
Align everyone to a few breakthrough goals.
Hoshin Kanri is a strategy deployment method that selects a few breakthrough objectives, translates them into goals and actions at each level, and reviews progress regularly.
Few priorities, deployed to every level.
Leadership & Daily Management
Policy Deployment
Connect strategy to daily work.
Policy deployment cascades goals and measures from the top down, with plans agreed through dialogue (catchball) between levels, so each team knows how its work supports the strategy.
Agree goals through dialogue, not decree.
Leadership & Daily Management
KPI vs KAI
Measure results and the activities that drive them.

A KPI (key performance indicator) measures results, such as OEE or OTIF. A KAI (key activity indicator) measures the improvement activities that drive those results, such as SMED events or audits completed.
Manage the activities to move the results.
Leadership & Daily Management
Leading vs Lagging Indicators
Predict the result versus report the result.
Leading indicators are measures that change before the outcome and can be influenced now, such as PM compliance. Lagging indicators show the outcome after the fact, such as breakdown hours.
Lead with what you can influence today.
Leadership & Daily Management
Accountability vs Blame
Own the process; do not blame the person.
Accountability means owning commitments and outcomes and following through. Blame focuses on finding someone at fault. A blame culture hides problems; an accountable culture surfaces and fixes them.
Ask 'what failed?' before 'who failed?'.
Leadership & Daily Management
Team Problem Solving
Solve problems together across roles.
Team problem solving uses the knowledge of operators, technicians, quality and supervisors together, with a simple structured method, to find causes and agree countermeasures.
The people closest to the problem solve it best.
Leadership & Daily Management
Cross-Functional Alignment
Different functions, one goal.
Cross-functional alignment means production, maintenance, quality, planning and supply chain agree shared goals, priorities and handoffs, so their actions support the whole value stream.
Shared goals beat department goals.
Leadership & Daily Management
Skill Matrix
Who can do what, and who needs training.
A skill matrix lists team members against the skills and tasks of the area, showing each person's level from 'in training' to 'can train others', to plan training and coverage.
Plan coverage before someone is absent.
Leadership & Daily Management
Training Within Industry
A proven method to train, improve and lead.

Training Within Industry (TWI) is a set of programs: Job Instruction (how to train), Job Methods (how to improve jobs) and Job Relations (how to lead people). Job Instruction uses four steps: prepare, present, try out, follow up.
If the learner has not learned, the instructor has not taught.
Leadership & Daily Management
Standardized Handover
Pass work over the same way every time.
A standardized handover uses a fixed format to pass on information between people or functions, such as status, issues, safety points and open actions, so nothing important is lost.
Same format, every handover.
Leadership & Daily Management
Shift Handover
Start the next shift fully informed.

A shift handover passes key information from the outgoing to the incoming shift: safety issues, quality concerns, equipment status, production status and open actions, ideally face to face at the line board.
Face to face, at the board, with a checklist.
Leadership & Daily Management
Meeting Waste
Meetings that waste time instead of creating value.
Meeting waste includes meetings without a purpose, agenda or decisions, the wrong people present, late starts and overruns, and actions that are never followed up.
Purpose, agenda, decisions, actions, on time.
Leadership & Daily Management
Decision Rights
Be clear about who decides what.
Decision rights define who makes which decisions, who must be consulted and who must be informed, so decisions are made quickly at the right level.
Decide at the lowest level with the right information.
Leadership & Daily Management
Management by Fact
Decide with data, not with opinions.
Management by fact means basing decisions on reliable data and direct observation rather than assumptions, while being clear about the quality and limits of the data.
In God we trust; all others bring data.
Leadership & Daily Management
Psychological Safety
People can speak up without fear.
Psychological safety is a shared belief that team members can raise problems, ask questions, admit mistakes and suggest ideas without fear of embarrassment or punishment.
Thank people for raising problems.
Leadership & Daily Management
Recognition for Kaizen
Recognize improvement to get more of it.
Recognition for kaizen acknowledges people's improvement ideas and efforts, publicly and promptly, which encourages continued participation. Recognition can be simple and does not need to be costly.
Recognize quickly, publicly and sincerely.
Leadership & Daily Management
Change Management
Help people move from the old way to the new.
Change management is a structured approach to help people adopt a new way of working: explain why, involve those affected, plan the transition, train, support and reinforce until the change sticks.
Explain why, involve early, support through.
Leadership & Daily Management
Resistance to Change
Resistance is information, not an enemy.
Resistance to change is a natural response when people feel uncertain, lose control or see risks. Listening to concerns, involving people and showing early results helps reduce it.
Listen to the resistance; it often points to a real risk.
Leadership & Daily Management
Leadership Case Study
An illustrative leadership change story.
A leadership case study shows how changes in leader routines and behaviour affected team performance. This example is illustrative; use your own observations and data in real cases.
Change the routine to change the culture.
Leadership & Daily Management
Daily Review Routine
A fixed daily routine to review performance.
A daily review routine is a set sequence at a fixed time: review yesterday's results against targets, discuss today's risks, agree actions and owners, and check previous actions.
Same time, same place, same agenda.
Leadership & Daily Management
Lean Culture
Shared habits of improvement and respect.
Lean culture is a workplace where people see problems as opportunities, follow and improve standards, go to the gemba, respect each other and improve every day as normal work.
Culture is what people do every day.
Leadership & Daily Management
Leadership Review
Routines, people and alignment.
Leadership review: build leader standard work and tiered meetings, use visual KPIs, escalate quickly, coach at the gemba, deploy strategy to every level, and create a culture where people speak up.
Lead with routines, coaching and respect.
Integrated Case Studies & Advanced Practice
End-to-End Lean Case Study
From value stream map to sustained results.

An end-to-end Lean case follows one product family from mapping the current state through the future state, implementation and sustainment. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Map, design, implement, sustain.
Integrated Case Studies & Advanced Practice
Packaging Line OEE Case
Use OEE losses to choose what to fix.
A packaging line OEE case breaks OEE into availability, performance and quality losses and targets the largest one first. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Fix the biggest loss first.
Integrated Case Studies & Advanced Practice
Changeover Reduction Case
Apply SMED to a real changeover.

A changeover reduction case films the current changeover, separates internal and external tasks, converts and streamlines them, then standardizes. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Film it, separate it, streamline it.
Integrated Case Studies & Advanced Practice
Material Shortage Case
Trace a shortage to its real cause.
A material shortage case investigates why material ran out and fixes the replenishment method, not just the immediate order. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Fix the replenishment system, not just the order.
Integrated Case Studies & Advanced Practice
Leakage Defect Case
Solve leakage with data and verified causes.
A leakage defect case uses stratification, cause analysis and verification to fix bottle leakage. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Stratify, verify, fix, control.
Integrated Case Studies & Advanced Practice
Labeling Defect Case
Error-proof the labelling step.
A labelling defect case addresses wrong or misplaced labels through root cause analysis and error-proofing. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Make the wrong label impossible to run.
Integrated Case Studies & Advanced Practice
Warehouse Flow Case
Shorten the paths in the warehouse.
A warehouse flow case uses spaghetti diagrams and slotting to reduce travel and picking errors. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Fast movers close to dispatch.
Integrated Case Studies & Advanced Practice
Batch Release Delay Case
Reduce waiting for batch release.
